title: Yudhishthira's half-truth
hookLine: a chariot that never touched the ground, a half-truth, and a verse for the tongue
carry: satya: say the true thing, kindly
tomorrow: same mistake, different punishment. what does the book do with that?

cards: Be honest: do you like my haircut? There's a half-second where your tongue decides. A kind lie is right there.
So is a hard truth. The Mahabharata tells of a man who never lied, until one day on a battlefield, and what it cost him.

teach.b: Yudhishthira was known for truth. In the epic, his chariot rode a little above the ground. In the great war, no one can stop the Pandavas' old teacher, Drona.
Krishna's plan: tell him his son Ashvatthama is dead. Bhima kills an elephant named Ashvatthama and shouts the news. Drona won't believe it unless Yudhishthira says it.
Yudhishthira says, aloud, Ashvatthama is dead, and adds, too low to hear, the elephant. Drona lays down his arms.
And Yudhishthira's chariot comes down onto the earth. True words, used to deceive: the epic marks it. That's satya, truthfulness, at the heart of Hindu dharma.
The Manusmriti puts it in one verse for the tongue, in paraphrase: say what is true; say what is pleasing; don't say a truth that wounds; and don't say a pleasing lie.
It opens satyam bruyat, priyam bruyat, and ends esha dharmah sanatanah, this is the eternal dharma, a phrase some Hindus use for their whole tradition.

teach.h: NO WOUNDING TRUTH, NO SWEET LIE.
teach.b: The verse closes both easy exits. What's left is a narrow road: the true thing, said so it can be heard. Read critically, it can't become a reason for silence while someone is wronged.
Ask whose comfort the silence protects.

how: The story of Yudhishthira's half-truth is often retold in Hindu homes as a lesson about satya, and the verse 'satyam bruyat priyam bruyat' is taught as a rule for speech, often without its source being named; some teachers add the critical question of when silence becomes a wrong.

o: a guide to chanting the Veda without mistakes
an old law book with a verse on true, kind speech
a book of proverbs gathered by a modern teacher

games.q: the speech verse — tap the pairs.
p: touched the earth after his half-truth

s: the verse says a kind lie is fine if it spares feelings
it rules out the pleasing lie as clearly as the wounding truth.
Yudhishthira's half-truth to Drona cost him nothing, since every word was true
his chariot, which had ridden above the ground, came down onto the earth.
the phrase 'sanatana dharma' closes a verse in the Manusmriti about speech
4.138 ends 'esha dharmah sanatanah': this is the eternal dharma.

games.q: a friend's band plays its first show. it wasn't good. after, she asks: be honest, were we good? what does Manu's speech verse point you to?
o: something true she can hear: what worked, and what to fix next.
'you were amazing!' kindness comes first, always.
'honestly? no.' truth comes first, however it lands.
games.why: the verse rules out both the pleasing lie and the wounding truth. what's left is the narrow road: true, and said so it can be heard.

practice: Bring to mind one true thing you've been meaning to tell someone, kind or hard. Say it quietly out loud, once, and listen to your own voice.
Then say it again, every word still true, letting the tone soften, and rest in the quiet after it until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The Manusmriti: the law book whose speech verse, satyam bruyat, asks for words both true and kind.

orig.note: Sanskrit, Manusmriti 4.138: say what is true, say what is pleasing.

carryVoice: Keep this one: satya, say the true thing, kindly. Yudhishthira's chariot touched the earth for a half-truth. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Drona Parva (Bhima kills the elephant Ashvatthama; Yudhishthira says Ashvatthama is slain, adding 'the elephant' indistinctly; his chariot, which had stood above the ground, touches the earth)
Manusmriti 4.138 (say what is true, say what is pleasing; no unpleasant truth, no pleasing falsehood; this is the eternal dharma)
